title: Biologics & Advanced Therapeutics
summary: Antibodies, fusion proteins, nucleic acid drugs, gene and cell therapy.

lessons.title: Monoclonal Antibodies

levels.kid:
Your body makes tiny Y-shaped helpers called antibodies. Each one has two little hands at the top that grab only one exact thing, like a key that fits just one lock.

Scientists learned to make huge batches of one exact antibody. These are called monoclonal antibodies, and they can be used as medicine!

Some grab a troublemaker and hold it so it can't cause harm. Some stick to bad cells and wave a flag so the body's guards come and attack them. Some block a door on a cell so a bad signal can't get in.

Their names often end in 'mab', which stands for monoclonal antibody.
levels.hs:
**Antibodies** are Y-shaped proteins made by B cells. The two tips (the **Fab** arms) bind one specific target, called an antigen. The stem (the **Fc** region) talks to immune cells and controls how long the antibody lasts in the blood.

**Monoclonal antibodies (mAbs)** are identical copies of one antibody, made in the lab. In 1975, Köhler and Milstein fused antibody-making cells with cancer cells to create **hybridomas**, cell lines that make one antibody forever (they won a Nobel Prize in 1984).

**How mAb drugs work:**
- **Neutralize** a signal molecule: adalimumab and infliximab block TNF in rheumatoid arthritis and Crohn's disease.
- **Block a receptor:** trastuzumab blocks HER2 on some tumors.
- **Mark cells for destruction:** rituximab binds CD20 on B cells.
- **Release the brakes on immunity:** checkpoint inhibitors like pembrolizumab (anti-PD-1) help T cells attack tumors.

**Naming:** mAb names end in **-mab**. Older names show the source: -omab (mouse), -ximab (chimeric), -zumab (humanized), -umab (fully human). Human-like antibodies cause fewer immune reactions.

mAbs are big proteins, so they can't be swallowed (digestion would destroy them). They are given by injection or infusion, and they last for weeks.
levels.college:
**Structure.** IgG has two heavy and two light chains. Variable domains contain three **complementarity-determining regions (CDRs)** per chain that form the paratope. The Fc region binds Fcγ receptors (FcγR), complement C1q and the neonatal Fc receptor (**FcRn**). Subclass matters:
- IgG1 has strong effector function (ADCC and CDC);
- IgG2 and IgG4 have weak effector function, used when only blockade is wanted;
- IgG4 undergoes Fab-arm exchange unless stabilized by the S228P hinge mutation.

**Engineering progression.** Murine antibodies caused human anti-mouse antibody (HAMA) responses, so the field moved to chimeric (mouse variable regions on human constant regions), humanized (CDR grafting) and fully human antibodies (from phage display or transgenic mice). Old INN infixes: -o-, -xi-, -zu-, -u-; target infixes such as -tu- (tumor), -li- (immune) and -ci- (cardiovascular). The source infix was dropped in 2017, and since 2022 new names use four suffixes in place of -mab: **-tug** (unmodified), **-bart** (artificial engineered), **-mig** (multispecific) and **-ment** (fragments).

**Mechanisms.** Ligand neutralization (anti-TNF, anti-VEGF bevacizumab, anti-IL-17, anti-CGRP fremanezumab), receptor blockade (anti-CGRP receptor erenumab, anti-EGFR cetuximab), effector-mediated killing (ADCC, ADCP, CDC; anti-CD20 rituximab and ocrelizumab), checkpoint blockade (PD-1, PD-L1, CTLA-4) and agonism (rarer).

**PK.**
- Subcutaneous absorption is slow, via lymphatics.
- Distribution is limited mostly to plasma and interstitial fluid; brain penetration is about 0.1% of plasma levels.
- Elimination is by proteolytic catabolism, not CYPs, and not renal filtration for intact IgG.
- **FcRn recycling** rescues IgG from lysosomal degradation, giving half-lives of about three weeks.
- **Target-mediated drug disposition** causes nonlinear PK at low concentrations.

**Class adverse effects.** Infusion reactions, immunogenicity (anti-drug antibodies), infections with immunosuppressive mAbs (TB reactivation with anti-TNF; PML with natalizumab), immune-related adverse events with checkpoint inhibitors, and ARIA with anti-amyloid antibodies (lecanemab, donanemab).
levels.phd:
**Fc engineering.**
- **Half-life extension:** the YTE (M252Y/S254T/T256E) and LS (M428L/N434S) mutations increase FcRn binding at acidic endosomal pH while preserving release at neutral pH, extending half-life severalfold (used in nirsevimab for RSV prevention and in long-acting anti-infectives).
- **Silencing:** LALA (L234A/L235A) and related mutations remove FcγR binding when effector function would be harmful (e.g., agonist or immune-checkpoint antibodies targeting T cells).
- **Enhancement:** afucosylation of the Asn297 glycan increases FcγRIIIa affinity and ADCC; obinutuzumab (anti-CD20) is glycoengineered this way. The S239D/I332E mutations enhance ADCC.

**Target-mediated drug disposition (TMDD).** With high-abundance or internalizing targets (e.g., EGFR, PD-L1 on tumors), binding and internalization act as a saturable clearance pathway. Clearance falls as concentrations rise and target is saturated, producing dose- and time-dependent PK. Cachexia and high tumor burden increase mAb clearance, partly explaining why patients with greater disease burden have lower exposure, which confounds exposure–response analyses.

**FcRn biology as a target.** FcRn antagonists (efgartigimod, rozanolixizumab) lower total IgG, including pathogenic autoantibodies, by blocking recycling. They are approved for generalized myasthenia gravis. The same mechanism shortens the half-life of co-administered therapeutic IgG.

**CNS delivery.** The blood–brain barrier restricts IgG. 'Brain shuttles' use bispecific formats that bind the transferrin receptor or other receptors to undergo transcytosis. Pabinafusp alfa (an anti-transferrin receptor antibody fused to an enzyme, approved in Japan) and trontinemab (an anti-amyloid shuttle in trials) illustrate the strategy, which needs careful tuning of affinity and valency to avoid lysosomal routing.

**ARIA mechanism.** Anti-amyloid antibodies binding vascular amyloid trigger inflammation and increased vessel permeability, causing edema (ARIA-E) and microhemorrhage or superficial siderosis (ARIA-H). Risk is highest in APOE ε4 homozygotes, which is why genotype counseling and MRI monitoring are part of treatment.
levels.expert:
**Clinical practice with mAbs.**
- **Screen before immunosuppressive biologics:** latent TB (interferon-gamma release assay), hepatitis B (surface antigen and core antibody; reactivation with anti-CD20 can be fatal), and vaccination status. Live vaccines are generally avoided during therapy.
- **Natalizumab and PML:** risk rises with anti-JC virus antibody positivity (and index), treatment duration over two years and prior immunosuppressants. Risk stratification, extended-interval dosing and MRI surveillance are standard in MS care.
- **Checkpoint inhibitors:** immune-related adverse events can affect any organ (colitis, hepatitis, pneumonitis, thyroiditis, hypophysitis, myocarditis, myositis, neurologic syndromes such as myasthenia-like presentations and encephalitis). Recognize early, hold therapy and treat with corticosteroids, escalating to other immunosuppressants. Myocarditis with myositis and myasthenia overlap is a high-mortality emergency.
- **Anti-amyloid antibodies:** check eligibility with amyloid confirmation, APOE genotyping with counseling, baseline MRI and scheduled MRIs during titration. Avoid in patients on anticoagulants or with many microbleeds, and know the ARIA management algorithm.

**Pharmacology pearls.**
- mAbs rarely have CYP-mediated interactions. However, cytokine-blocking mAbs (e.g., anti-IL-6) can restore suppressed CYP activity in inflamed patients and lower levels of co-administered CYP substrates such as warfarin or ciclosporin.
- **Therapeutic drug monitoring** with trough levels and anti-drug antibodies guides anti-TNF therapy in IBD after loss of response: low drug without antibodies suggests intensifying; low drug with high antibodies suggests switching.

**Reading a name.** In older names, infixes give hints: 'tu' (tumor), 'li' or 'lim' (immune), 'ne' (nervous system, e.g., aducanumab, tanezumab) and 'ci' (cardiovascular). Remember that the naming scheme changed, so newer agents may not follow these rules.

keyPoints: Antibody = 2 Fab arms (binding via CDRs) + Fc (effector function, FcRn recycling)
Hybridoma technology (Köhler & Milstein, 1975) made monoclonal antibodies possible
Old naming: -omab (mouse), -ximab (chimeric), -zumab (humanized), -umab (human); new suffixes since 2022: -tug, -bart, -mig, -ment
Mechanisms: neutralization, receptor blockade, ADCC/CDC killing, checkpoint blockade
FcRn recycling → ~3-week half-lives; elimination by catabolism, not CYPs
Key risks: infusion reactions, infections (TB, HBV, PML), immune-related adverse events, ARIA

lessons.title: Fusion Proteins and Antibody–Drug Conjugates

levels.kid:
Scientists love to build medicines like LEGO. They take useful pieces and snap them together.

One trick is a fusion protein. They take a piece that grabs a troublemaker and snap it onto the long-lasting stem of an antibody. Now the grabber stays in the body much longer.

Another trick is called an antibody–drug conjugate. Imagine a guided missile: the antibody is the guidance system that finds cancer cells, and a tiny, super-strong poison is tied on top. The antibody carries the poison straight to the cancer cell, so healthy cells are mostly left alone.
levels.hs:
Biologic drugs can be built from parts, like modules.

**Fusion proteins** join two proteins into one molecule. Often, a receptor or other binding piece is attached to the **Fc** stem of an antibody, which makes it last much longer in the blood.
- **Etanercept:** TNF receptor + Fc. It soaks up TNF to treat rheumatoid arthritis and psoriasis.
- **Abatacept:** CTLA-4 + Fc. It blocks the 'second signal' T cells need to switch on.
- **Aflibercept:** a VEGF 'trap' that treats eye diseases with leaky blood vessels.

**Bispecific antibodies** grab two different targets at once. **Blinatumomab** links T cells (CD3) to leukemia cells (CD19) so the T cells kill them. **Emicizumab** bridges two clotting factors to replace missing factor VIII in hemophilia A.

**Antibody–drug conjugates (ADCs)** are 'guided missiles' with three parts:
1. an **antibody** that finds a target on cancer cells (like HER2);
2. a **linker** that holds the drug on;
3. a very potent **payload**, a cell-killing drug too toxic to give on its own.

The ADC binds the cancer cell, gets pulled inside, and releases its payload. Examples: **trastuzumab deruxtecan** and **brentuximab vedotin**. Side effects still happen, often caused by the payload, like nerve damage, low blood counts or lung inflammation.
levels.college:
**Fc-fusion proteins.** Fusing a binding domain to IgG Fc adds FcRn-mediated half-life extension and dimerization (which increases avidity).
- Etanercept (TNFR2–Fc) binds TNF and lymphotoxin-α; unlike anti-TNF mAbs, it is ineffective in Crohn's disease and granulomatous disease.
- Abatacept (CTLA-4–Ig) binds CD80/86 and blocks CD28 co-stimulation; belatacept is a higher-affinity version used in kidney transplantation.
- Aflibercept (VEGFR1/VEGFR2–Fc) traps VEGF-A, VEGF-B and PlGF.
- Romiplostim is a 'peptibody' (thrombopoietin-mimetic peptides on Fc).
- Other half-life strategies: albumin fusion or binding, PEGylation and XTEN/PAS polypeptides.

**Bispecifics.**
- **T-cell engagers:** blinatumomab is a BiTE (two scFvs, no Fc) with a half-life of hours, requiring continuous infusion; newer Fc-bearing CD3 bispecifics (teclistamab, glofitamab, tarlatamab) allow intermittent dosing. Their key toxicities are **cytokine release syndrome** and **ICANS** (neurotoxicity).
- **Emicizumab** bridges factor IXa and factor X, mimicking factor VIII cofactor activity, and works even in patients with factor VIII inhibitors.

**ADC design.**
- **Antibody:** a target highly expressed on tumors, limited on normal tissue, internalizing.
- **Linker:** cleavable (protease-sensitive valine–citrulline cut by cathepsin B, acid-labile hydrazone, or reducible disulfide) or non-cleavable (thioether, which needs full antibody degradation, e.g., trastuzumab emtansine, T-DM1).
- **Payload:** microtubule inhibitors (MMAE, MMAF, DM1, DM4), DNA damagers (calicheamicin, PBD dimers) or topoisomerase I inhibitors (deruxtecan, SN-38).
- **DAR (drug-to-antibody ratio)** is typically about 2 to 8. Higher DAR raises potency but can speed clearance and toxicity.

**Bystander effect.** Membrane-permeable payloads released from cleavable linkers (MMAE, DXd) diffuse into neighboring cells, killing target-negative tumor cells in heterogeneous tumors. Charged payloads (MMAF, lysine-MCC-DM1) do not. This helps explain trastuzumab deruxtecan's activity in 'HER2-low' tumors.

**Toxicity is often payload-driven:** neuropathy (MMAE), ocular toxicity (MMAF, DM4), interstitial lung disease (deruxtecan), neutropenia and diarrhea (SN-38), and hepatic veno-occlusive disease (calicheamicin).
levels.phd:
**ADC pharmacokinetics.** An ADC is a mixture of species with different DARs. Analysts track three analytes: total antibody, conjugated antibody (or antibody-conjugated payload) and free payload. Deconjugation in circulation (e.g., retro-Michael reaction of maleimide–thiol linkages exchanging the drug-linker onto albumin) lowers efficacy and releases free payload systemically. Self-hydrolyzing maleimides and site-specific conjugation were developed to fix this.

**Conjugation chemistry.** First-generation ADCs used stochastic conjugation to lysines or reduced interchain cysteines, giving heterogeneous DAR distributions. High-DAR species clear faster (hydrophobicity-driven uptake by the liver). Site-specific methods produce homogeneous products with wider therapeutic windows:
- engineered cysteines (THIOMABs);
- non-natural amino acids;
- enzymatic tagging (transglutaminase, sortase);
- glycan remodeling.

**Mylotarg's history.** Gemtuzumab ozogamicin (anti-CD33–calicheamicin) received accelerated approval in 2000. It was withdrawn in 2010 after a confirmatory trial showed no benefit and more early deaths, partly attributed to an unstable hydrazone linker and the regimen used. It was re-approved in 2017 with a fractionated regimen, which shows how schedule and exposure shape the therapeutic window.

**Mechanistic frontiers.**
- **Immune-stimulating antibody conjugates** (TLR7/8 or STING agonist payloads).
- **Degrader-antibody conjugates** delivering PROTACs.
- **Bispecific ADCs** that improve internalization or tumor selectivity.
- **Radioligand and radio-antibody conjugates**, which share the same targeting logic.

Resistance mechanisms include antigen loss, impaired internalization or lysosomal processing, and upregulation of payload efflux pumps (e.g., ABCB1 for MMAE).

**T-cell engager biology.** The efficacy of CD3 bispecifics depends on the immune synapse geometry, set by the epitope's distance from the membrane and the format's size. Cytokine release follows T-cell activation kinetics, which is the rationale for step-up dosing and corticosteroid premedication. Tocilizumab (anti-IL-6 receptor) treats CRS, while ICANS reflects endothelial activation and blood–brain barrier disruption and responds to corticosteroids rather than IL-6 blockade.
levels.expert:
**Practical management.**
- **Interstitial lung disease with trastuzumab deruxtecan:** educate patients to report cough, breathlessness or fever. Image promptly. Hold the drug for any grade, and stop permanently for symptomatic ILD while starting corticosteroids. Early detection changes outcomes.
- **Peripheral neuropathy with MMAE-based ADCs** (brentuximab vedotin, enfortumab vedotin, polatuzumab vedotin) is cumulative, so assess at each cycle and modify early to avoid permanent disability. Enfortumab vedotin also causes serious skin reactions and hyperglycemia.
- **Ocular toxicity** (keratopathy with belantamab mafodotin; blurred vision with mirvetuximab soravtansine) requires baseline and ongoing eye examinations and lubricating drops.
- **Sacituzumab govitecan** carries severe neutropenia and diarrhea warnings, with increased risk in UGT1A1*28 homozygotes.

**T-cell engagers.**
- Use step-up dosing and premedication, and monitor during initial doses (often inpatient).
- Grade CRS by fever, hypotension and hypoxia (ASTCT criteria). Give tocilizumab for moderate to severe CRS and add corticosteroids if refractory.
- Assess ICANS with the ICE score (orientation, naming, following commands, writing, attention). Treat with corticosteroids and seizure precautions.
- Infection risk rises from B-cell aplasia and hypogammaglobulinemia with CD19, CD20 and BCMA engagers. Immunoglobulin replacement and prophylaxis may be needed.

**Fusion proteins.**
- Etanercept is less effective than anti-TNF mAbs in IBD and granulomatous inflammation, which matters when choosing a TNF blocker for a patient with both psoriasis and Crohn's disease.
- Emicizumab interferes with aPTT-based assays, including one-stage factor VIII activity, so labs must use chromogenic assays with bovine reagents. When bypassing agents are used for breakthrough bleeding, avoid activated prothrombin complex concentrate where possible, because combination with emicizumab has caused thrombotic microangiopathy.

**Thinking like an oncologist about ADCs.** Ask: what is the target expression (including 'low' categories), which payload class is it, and has the patient already had that payload class (cross-resistance)? Consider overlapping toxicities with prior therapy, such as baseline neuropathy before an MMAE ADC.

keyPoints: Fc-fusion proteins (etanercept, abatacept, aflibercept) gain FcRn half-life and avidity
Bispecifics: blinatumomab (CD19×CD3 T-cell engager), emicizumab (factor VIII mimic)
ADC = antibody + linker (cleavable or non-cleavable) + potent payload; DAR ≈ 2–8
Bystander effect: membrane-permeable payloads (MMAE, DXd) kill neighboring cells
ADC toxicity is often payload-driven: neuropathy (MMAE), ILD (deruxtecan), ocular (MMAF/DM4)
T-cell engagers cause CRS (treat with tocilizumab) and ICANS (treat with corticosteroids)

lessons.title: Antisense, siRNA and mRNA

levels.kid:
Inside your cells, your genes send out little message notes called RNA. The notes tell the cell which proteins to build.

Some new medicines work on those notes!

Antisense medicines are like a sticky note that covers part of the message, so the cell reads it differently or throws it away.

siRNA medicines hand the message to a tiny shredder in the cell, so the bad protein never gets made.

mRNA medicines are new message notes the doctor gives you, so your cells build a helpful protein, like a 'wanted poster' that trains your body to fight a virus.
levels.hs:
Most drugs act on proteins. **Nucleic acid drugs** act one step earlier, on **RNA**, the message copied from DNA that tells cells which protein to make.

**Antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs)** are short, single strands of modified DNA- or RNA-like building blocks that stick to a matching RNA sequence. Depending on the design, they either trigger destruction of the RNA or change how it is spliced (cut and pasted). **Nusinersen** changes splicing of the SMN2 gene to make working SMN protein in **spinal muscular atrophy (SMA)**. It is injected into the spinal fluid because it can't cross the blood–brain barrier.

**Small interfering RNAs (siRNAs)** are short double strands. Inside the cell, one strand guides a protein complex called **RISC** to cut the matching messenger RNA, silencing the gene. **Patisiran** (2018, the first approved siRNA) silences transthyretin in a nerve-damaging amyloid disease. **Inclisiran** silences PCSK9 to lower LDL cholesterol and only needs to be given a couple of times a year.

**mRNA drugs** deliver a message that cells translate into a protein. The COVID-19 vaccines (2020) used mRNA wrapped in **lipid nanoparticles**. A chemical tweak, swapping uridine for a modified version, stops the immune system from overreacting to the RNA.

The big challenge for all of these is **delivery**: getting fragile RNA into the right cells.
levels.college:
**ASOs (typically about 16 to 20 nucleotides).**
- **RNase H1 'gapmers':** a central DNA gap flanked by modified RNA-like wings. The DNA:RNA hybrid recruits RNase H1, which cleaves the target RNA (e.g., tofersen for SOD1-ALS, inotersen for hereditary transthyretin amyloidosis).
- **Steric blockers:** fully modified, no RNase H. They modulate splicing or translation. Nusinersen promotes SMN2 exon 7 inclusion; eteplirsen and related morpholinos induce DMD exon skipping to restore the reading frame (accelerated approvals based on dystrophin expression).
- **Chemistry:** phosphorothioate backbone (nuclease resistance, protein binding that slows renal loss), 2′-O-methoxyethyl (2′-MOE), 2′-O-methyl, locked nucleic acids/constrained ethyl (higher affinity), and phosphorodiamidate morpholinos (neutral backbone).

**siRNAs (about 21 base pairs).** The guide (antisense) strand loads into Argonaute-2 within RISC and directs cleavage of fully complementary mRNA. The passenger strand is discarded. Catalytic turnover and RISC stability give long-lasting knockdown.
- **Delivery:** lipid nanoparticles (patisiran) or **GalNAc conjugates**, which bind the asialoglycoprotein receptor on hepatocytes, allowing subcutaneous dosing (givosiran, lumasiran, inclisiran, vutrisiran).
- Heavy 2′-F/2′-OMe modification and stabilization chemistry extend the duration of effect to months.

**mRNA therapeutics.** These include a 5′ cap, UTRs, the coding sequence and a poly(A) tail. **N1-methylpseudouridine** reduces recognition by TLR7/8 and other sensors and increases translation. **Lipid nanoparticles** (ionizable lipid, cholesterol, helper phospholipid, PEG-lipid) protect the RNA, are taken up by endocytosis, and release RNA when the ionizable lipid becomes protonated in the acidic endosome. Applications include vaccines (infectious disease, personalized cancer vaccines) and protein replacement (in trials).

**Toxicities.** ASOs: thrombocytopenia (inotersen), kidney toxicity, injection-site reactions; intrathecal procedure risks. siRNAs: generally well tolerated; injection-site reactions. mRNA vaccines: reactogenicity, and rare myocarditis, mostly in young males after the second dose.
levels.phd:
**Pharmacology of oligonucleotides.** Phosphorothioate ASOs bind plasma proteins extensively, distribute widely to liver, kidney and bone marrow, and are taken up by cells via endocytosis. Only a small fraction escapes endosomes to reach its target (productive uptake), which is the major efficiency bottleneck for all nucleic acid drugs. Tissue half-lives are weeks to months, so effects outlast plasma levels. Stereochemistry matters: each phosphorothioate creates a chiral center, and stereopure ASOs are being developed to optimize activity.

**Off-target and class effects.** Hybridization-dependent off-targets arise from partial complementarity to other transcripts. Hybridization-independent effects come from protein binding (complement activation, platelet effects). For siRNAs, **seed-region-mediated off-targeting** (miRNA-like repression via guide nucleotides 2–8) is a key concern, mitigated by thermal destabilization of the seed (e.g., the glycol nucleic acid modification in enhanced stabilization chemistry designs).

**CNS delivery.** Intrathecal ASOs distribute along the neuraxis but reach deep brain structures less well. Antibody–oligonucleotide conjugates targeting the transferrin receptor and lipid-conjugated siRNAs are being explored to reach brain parenchyma after systemic dosing.

**Tofersen and surrogate endpoints.** In the VALOR trial, tofersen lowered CSF SOD1 and plasma neurofilament light chain (NfL) but missed its primary clinical endpoint at 28 weeks; open-label extension data suggested benefit with earlier treatment. It received accelerated approval in 2023 based on NfL reduction, an influential precedent for biomarker-based approval in neurodegeneration.

**Personalized ASOs.** Milasen (2018), designed for a single child with a unique splice mutation causing Batten disease, showed that individualized ASOs can be developed in about a year. This raises new regulatory, ethical and N-of-1 trial design questions now being addressed through dedicated frameworks.

**mRNA innate sensing.** Unmodified in vitro transcribed RNA activates TLR3, TLR7/8, RIG-I, MDA5 and PKR, causing interferon responses and translational shutdown. Nucleoside modification plus purification to remove double-stranded RNA byproducts made therapeutic mRNA feasible. Self-amplifying RNA (encoding a viral replicase) achieves expression at lower doses but re-introduces innate sensing challenges.
levels.expert:
**Clinical use in neurology.**
- **Nusinersen** is given by repeated intrathecal injection with loading then maintenance intervals. In patients with scoliosis or spinal fusion, imaging-guided access may be needed. Monitor platelets, coagulation and urine protein (a class effect of antisense drugs). The SMA treatment landscape now includes gene therapy (onasemnogene abeparvovec) and oral splicing modifiers (risdiplam), so drug choice depends on age, SMN2 copy number, access and family preference.
- **Tofersen** for SOD1-ALS requires genetic confirmation of a SOD1 mutation. Monitor for serious neurologic adverse events (myelitis, radiculitis, papilledema and raised intracranial pressure, aseptic meningitis) and CSF changes.
- **Patisiran and vutrisiran** for hereditary transthyretin amyloidosis polyneuropathy reduce vitamin A transport (TTR carries retinol-binding protein), so vitamin A supplementation is recommended. Inotersen needs frequent platelet and kidney monitoring because of thrombocytopenia and glomerulonephritis risk.

**Cardiometabolic.** Inclisiran's infrequent, clinic-administered dosing improves adherence. It lowers LDL similarly to PCSK9 antibodies, but hard outcome trial data were still pending when it was approved, which is relevant when choosing between agents.

**Counseling points.**
- These drugs do not change DNA. ASOs and siRNAs act on RNA, and their effect wears off, so ongoing dosing is needed.
- mRNA is degraded within days and does not enter the nucleus or integrate into the genome.

**Myocarditis after mRNA vaccination.** It is rare, typically within a week of the second dose, mostly in adolescent and young adult males, and usually mild with rapid recovery. Recognize chest pain, palpitations or breathlessness, check troponin and ECG, and refer to cardiology.

**Thinking ahead.** When evaluating a new oligonucleotide, ask: what tissue must it reach, and how (GalNAc to liver, intrathecal to CNS, LNP)? Is the mechanism knockdown or splice modulation? Is the target mutation-specific (allele-selective) or total? And what biomarker shows target engagement (e.g., CSF SOD1, serum TTR, LDL)?

keyPoints: ASOs: single-stranded; RNase H gapmers degrade RNA, steric blockers change splicing (nusinersen for SMA)
siRNAs: double-stranded; the guide strand directs RISC/Ago2 to cleave target mRNA
GalNAc conjugates target hepatocytes via ASGPR; LNPs deliver patisiran and mRNA
mRNA drugs: N1-methylpseudouridine reduces innate immune sensing (2023 Nobel)
CNS oligonucleotides (nusinersen, tofersen) are given intrathecally
These drugs do not alter DNA; delivery and endosomal escape are the key hurdles

lessons.title: Gene Therapy

levels.kid:
Some people are born with a typo in one of their gene recipes. Because of the typo, their body can't make an important protein, and they get sick.

Gene therapy tries to fix that. Scientists take a harmless virus, empty out the parts that make people sick, and put a correct copy of the recipe inside. The virus works like a delivery truck that drops the good recipe into the right cells.

Another way is like a word processor: tools such as CRISPR can find the typo and edit it.

Sometimes doctors even take out a person's own cells, fix them, and put them back.
levels.hs:
**Gene therapy** treats disease by adding, fixing or switching off genes in a patient's cells.

**Two ways to do it:**
- **In vivo:** the gene is delivered directly into the body, for example by an injection into the blood, eye or spinal fluid.
- **Ex vivo:** cells (often blood stem cells or T cells) are removed, modified in the lab, and returned to the patient.

**Viral vectors** are viruses with their disease-causing genes removed, used as delivery trucks:
- **AAV (adeno-associated virus):** mostly stays outside the chromosomes; used in **onasemnogene abeparvovec**, a one-time infusion for babies with spinal muscular atrophy, and **voretigene neparvovec**, injected under the retina for an inherited blindness.
- **Lentivirus:** inserts its genes into the chromosomes, so the change is passed on when cells divide; used for ex vivo stem cell therapies.

**Gene editing** with **CRISPR-Cas9** cuts DNA at a chosen spot. **Exa-cel** (Casgevy), approved in 2023, edits patients' blood stem cells so they make fetal hemoglobin, treating sickle cell disease and beta-thalassemia.

**CAR-T cells** are a patient's T cells given a new receptor that recognizes cancer cells, like CD19 on leukemia cells.

**Risks** include immune reactions to the vector, liver injury, inserting genes in the wrong place (which can cause cancer), and very high costs.
levels.college:
**Vectors.**
- **AAV:** small single-stranded DNA virus; packaging capacity about 4.7 kb. Mostly forms non-integrating episomes, giving durable expression in non-dividing cells (neurons, muscle, retina, liver) but dilution in dividing cells. Serotypes and engineered capsids determine tropism (AAV9 crosses the blood–brain barrier in infants, the basis for IV onasemnogene). Pre-existing neutralizing antibodies to the capsid often exclude patients, and redosing is generally not possible because therapy induces strong antibodies.
- **Lentivirus:** integrating, about 8 kb capacity, transduces non-dividing cells; mainly ex vivo hematopoietic stem cell (HSC) and CAR-T products.
- **Gamma-retrovirus:** integrating, dividing cells only. Early SCID-X1 trials caused leukemias from insertional activation of LMO2, leading to self-inactivating vector designs.
- **Adenovirus:** high capacity and strongly immunogenic; now used mainly in vaccines and oncolytic therapy.
- **Non-viral:** lipid nanoparticles delivering CRISPR components to the liver.

**Gene editing.** Cas9 creates double-strand breaks repaired by non-homologous end joining (gene disruption) or homology-directed repair (precise correction, inefficient). **Base editors** (deaminase + Cas9 nickase) make C→T or A→G changes without double-strand breaks; **prime editors** (reverse transcriptase + nickase + pegRNA) write small edits. Exa-cel disrupts the erythroid-specific enhancer of BCL11A, a repressor of fetal γ-globin, so patients produce HbF.

**CAR-T.** Autologous T cells are transduced with a chimeric antigen receptor (scFv + hinge + transmembrane + CD3ζ + co-stimulatory domain such as CD28 or 4-1BB). Targets include CD19 (tisagenlecleucel, 2017) and BCMA. Patients receive lymphodepleting chemotherapy before infusion. Toxicities: cytokine release syndrome (tocilizumab), ICANS (corticosteroids), B-cell aplasia, prolonged cytopenias, and rare secondary T-cell malignancies (FDA boxed warning, 2024).

**Safety signals with AAV.** High systemic doses cause hepatotoxicity (requiring corticosteroid prophylaxis), complement-mediated thrombotic microangiopathy, myocarditis, and dorsal root ganglion toxicity in animal studies. Deaths have occurred in high-dose trials.
levels.expert:
**Bedside considerations.**
- **Onasemnogene abeparvovec:** confirm anti-AAV9 antibody titer below the label threshold. Give prophylactic corticosteroids and monitor liver tests, platelets, troponin and kidney function for weeks afterwards (risks: acute liver injury, including fatal liver failure, and thrombotic microangiopathy). Treating early, ideally before symptoms after newborn screening, gives the best motor outcomes because lost motor neurons cannot be recovered.
- **Voretigene neparvovec** requires confirmed biallelic RPE65 mutations and enough viable retinal cells. It is delivered by vitrectomy and subretinal injection in specialized centers.
- **Exa-cel** requires stem cell mobilization and collection, then myeloablative busulfan conditioning. Patients face prolonged cytopenias, infection risk and the long-term effects of conditioning chemotherapy, plus long hospitalization. Counseling must weigh these against disease severity and alternatives such as allogeneic transplant.

**CAR-T logistics and toxicity.** Bridging therapy is needed during manufacturing. After infusion, patients stay near the treatment center for weeks and must not drive for about two months because of delayed neurotoxicity risk. Use CRS and ICANS grading (ASTCT) with algorithm-driven tocilizumab and corticosteroids, and seizure prophylaxis per center protocol. Late effects: hypogammaglobulinemia (immunoglobulin replacement), cytopenias, infections and monitoring for secondary malignancies.

**Neurosurgical relevance.** Several CNS gene therapies are delivered by stereotactic neurosurgery: intraputaminal AAV-AADC (eladocagene exuparvovec, approved in the EU and US for AADC deficiency), and trials in Parkinson's disease and Huntington's disease. Delivery uses real-time MRI-guided convection-enhanced infusion to confirm coverage of the target structure. The surgeon's technique (cannula design, infusion rate, avoiding reflux along the track) directly determines efficacy.

**Ethics.** Gene therapy in children requires careful consent about irreversibility, unknown long-term effects and long-term follow-up obligations. Editing embryos for clinical use is prohibited in most countries. Equity of access is a major concern given cost and specialized infrastructure.

keyPoints: In vivo (vector into the body) vs ex vivo (cells modified outside, then returned)
AAV: small (~4.7 kb), mostly non-integrating; AAV9 used IV for SMA (onasemnogene)
Lentivirus integrates: used for ex vivo HSC and CAR-T products; insertional oncogenesis is a risk
CRISPR exa-cel disrupts the BCL11A enhancer to raise fetal hemoglobin (sickle cell, β-thalassemia)
CAR-T: CRS (tocilizumab), ICANS (corticosteroids), B-cell aplasia
AAV toxicities: hepatotoxicity, thrombotic microangiopathy; pre-existing antibodies exclude patients

kidTest.explain: A mistake in the gene.

kidTest.q: CRISPR is like a...
kidTest.explain: It finds and changes DNA.

kidTest.explain: That's ex vivo gene therapy.

choices: No, the sickness parts are removed

choices: Capsid-specific CD8+ T cells killing transduced hepatocytes
advancedTest.explain: Corticosteroids are used to blunt it.

advancedTest.explain: Base and prime editors aim to avoid DSBs.

choices: To confirm the infusate covers the target and avoid reflux along the cannula track
advancedTest.explain: Surgical delivery technique determines efficacy.

lessons.title: Biosimilars and Immunogenicity

levels.kid:
Some medicines are tiny and simple, like a paper airplane. Anyone with the instructions can fold an exact copy.

Biologic medicines are huge and are made by living cells, like a cake baked by yeast. Even with the same recipe, every bakery's cake is a tiny bit different.

So copies of biologics are called biosimilars: 'very, very similar' but not perfectly identical. Scientists test them a lot to prove they work just as well and are just as safe.

Another thing: because biologics are big proteins, the body's guards sometimes notice them and make antibodies against them. Then the medicine may stop working.
levels.hs:
**Biologics** are medicines made in living cells: antibodies, hormones like insulin, enzymes and more. They are big, complex molecules, often with sugar chains attached. Small-molecule drugs can be copied exactly as **generics**, but biologics can't, because tiny differences in cells and manufacturing change the final product.

A **biosimilar** is a biologic that is **highly similar** to an approved original (the 'reference product'), with **no clinically meaningful differences** in safety, purity or potency. To prove this, manufacturers mostly use detailed lab analysis of structure and function, plus studies comparing blood levels and often a clinical trial.

Biosimilars are usually cheaper and increase access. The first US biosimilar, filgrastim-sndz, was approved in 2015; Europe approved its first in 2006. US biosimilar names have a four-letter suffix, like infliximab-dyyb.

**Immunogenicity** means a drug triggers an immune response. The body can make **anti-drug antibodies (ADAs)** against a biologic. These can:
- make the drug stop working (neutralizing antibodies, or faster clearance);
- cause infusion reactions or allergic reactions;
- rarely, cross-react with the body's own version of the protein.

For example, people with severe hemophilia A can develop 'inhibitors' against the factor VIII they are given. Taking methotrexate alongside some anti-TNF antibodies lowers the chance of making ADAs.
levels.college:
**Why biologics vary.** Post-translational modifications (glycosylation, deamidation, oxidation), charge variants, aggregation and host-cell impurities depend on the cell line and process. Even an originator's own product shifts slightly after manufacturing changes, which are managed by **comparability** exercises. The adage 'the process is the product' captures this.

**Biosimilarity: totality of evidence.** The evidence forms a stepwise pyramid:
- extensive analytical characterization (primary sequence must be identical; higher-order structure, glycan profile, binding assays);
- functional assays (target binding, Fc functions such as ADCC);
- comparative PK (and PD where possible) in healthy volunteers or patients;
- a comparative clinical study in a sensitive population and endpoint, where needed, plus immunogenicity assessment.

Regulators now accept that strong analytical similarity can reduce or remove the need for comparative efficacy trials. **Extrapolation** allows approval for the reference product's other indications without separate trials when the mechanism is shared and justified.

**Regulation.** In the EU, the biosimilar framework dates from 2005, with the first approval (somatropin) in 2006. In the US, the BPCI Act (2009, part of the Affordable Care Act) created the 351(k) pathway. Reference products receive 12 years of exclusivity. **Interchangeability** is a US designation allowing pharmacy-level substitution without prescriber involvement (subject to state law); FDA draft guidance (2024) indicates switching studies are generally not needed.

**Immunogenicity determinants.**
- **Product:** non-human sequences, aggregates (strongly immunogenic), impurities, glycan structures, formulation, container leachables.
- **Patient:** disease, genetics (HLA), concomitant immunosuppression, prior exposure.
- **Treatment:** route (subcutaneous more immunogenic than IV), intermittent versus continuous exposure, duration.

**Assays.** A tiered approach: screening (bridging ELISA or electrochemiluminescence), confirmatory (drug competition), titer and neutralizing assays. Drug tolerance matters: circulating drug can mask ADAs.

**Consequences.** Loss of response (anti-TNF), hypersensitivity, and neutralization of endogenous protein.
levels.phd:
**Eprex and pure red cell aplasia.** Around 1998–2004, cases of antibody-mediated pure red cell aplasia surged in patients with chronic kidney disease receiving a subcutaneous epoetin alfa formulation (Eprex) outside the US. The trigger was traced to a formulation change: human serum albumin was replaced by polysorbate 80, and organic compounds leaching from uncoated rubber syringe stoppers likely acted as adjuvants or promoted micelle-associated epoetin presentation. The antibodies neutralized endogenous erythropoietin as well, causing transfusion-dependent anemia. Changes to stoppers and the route of administration largely resolved it. This is the paradigm case of a manufacturing change creating immunogenicity, and the reason post-approval comparability and pharmacovigilance for biologics are rigorous.

**PEG-MGDF.** A pegylated truncated thrombopoietin elicited antibodies cross-reacting with endogenous thrombopoietin, causing thrombocytopenia, and development stopped. Romiplostim was designed with no sequence homology to thrombopoietin partly to avoid this.

**Mechanisms of ADA formation.** Responses to foreign proteins follow classic T-cell-dependent pathways with high-affinity, class-switched antibodies. For human-sequence proteins, B-cell tolerance can be broken when aggregates present repetitive epitopes that cross-link B-cell receptors (a T-independent-like mechanism). In silico T-cell epitope prediction and de-immunization (removing MHC class II binding peptides) guide protein engineering.

**Pre-existing antibodies.** **Cetuximab** anaphylaxis on first infusion clustered in the southeastern US because of pre-existing IgE against galactose-α-1,3-galactose (alpha-gal) on the Fab, produced by the murine SP2/0 cell line. Sensitization is linked to lone star tick bites, the same mechanism behind delayed red-meat allergy. Anti-PEG antibodies, present in a portion of the population, can accelerate clearance of PEGylated drugs and cause hypersensitivity.

**Clinical immunogenicity data are product-specific.** ADA incidences cannot be compared across products or assays, since sensitivity, drug tolerance and cut points differ. Labels therefore warn against cross-product comparison.
levels.expert:
**Switching and prescribing biosimilars.** Large randomized switching studies (e.g., NOR-SWITCH for infliximab) and real-world cohorts show no loss of efficacy or safety when stable patients switch from originator to biosimilar. A 'nocebo' effect (patients expecting worse outcomes after a switch) can cause subjective worsening and discontinuation, so clear communication matters: explain that the biosimilar is the same active molecule within tight quality limits and is as rigorously regulated. Record brand and batch for traceability in pharmacovigilance.

**Managing immunogenicity in practice.**
- **Anti-TNF therapy in IBD and rheumatology:** combination with an immunomodulator (azathioprine or methotrexate) lowers ADA formation and improves durability, as shown in trials such as SONIC. Avoid episodic dosing, and consider proactive therapeutic drug monitoring in selected patients.
- **Reactive TDM interpretation:** adequate drug level plus active disease suggests a mechanistic failure, so switch class. Low drug without ADAs: intensify. Low drug with high-titer ADAs: switch within class or out of class. Note that ADAs against one anti-TNF do not cross-react with another, so a within-class switch is reasonable after immunogenic failure.
- **Infusion reactions:** many are not IgE-mediated. Slowing the rate and premedication are common responses. True anaphylaxis needs immediate management and generally stopping the drug.
- **Hemophilia A inhibitors:** they occur in a substantial minority of previously untreated patients with severe disease, mostly within the first exposure days. Management includes bypassing agents, emicizumab prophylaxis (unaffected by factor VIII inhibitors) and immune tolerance induction.
- **Neurology:** neutralizing antibodies to interferon-beta reduce efficacy in MS; persistent anti-natalizumab antibodies cause loss of efficacy and infusion reactions, so testing is indicated for reactions or breakthrough disease.

**Cetuximab tip.** In high-prevalence regions, some centers screen for alpha-gal IgE before the first infusion, a practical example of how pre-existing immunity changes risk.

**Bottom line.** Biosimilars expand access safely. Immunogenicity is a property of the product, the patient and the treatment together, so it must be monitored throughout a biologic's life.

keyPoints: Biologics are made in living cells and cannot be copied exactly: 'the process is the product'
Biosimilar = highly similar, no clinically meaningful differences; proven by totality of evidence (analytics first)
Extrapolation across indications and (US) interchangeability designation
Anti-drug antibodies cause loss of response, infusion reactions, rarely neutralization of the endogenous protein
Eprex: a formulation change → antibodies against epoetin and endogenous EPO → pure red cell aplasia
Methotrexate/azathioprine with anti-TNF lowers ADA formation; alpha-gal IgE → cetuximab anaphylaxis
